catalog_quote: [Odden 1979:159-160, quoting Sapir & Swadesh 1960:4] The same rule is encountered in Yana, according to Sapir and Swadesh (1960): "The word stress, variable to some extent, tends to fall on the first heavy syllable, that is, on the first syllable which is either closed with a consonant or which contains a vowel cluster. Where there is no heavy syllable, the first syllable tends to carry the stress." ... [Sapir & Swadesh 1960, phonology section, rule (6), Rosetta/archive.org page] (6) Double vowels are simplified when they come to stand in closed syllables; thus, by vowel mutation, /a/ becomes doubled /oo/ in wookui- "to sew" (from wakui-) but single vowel in ... "to kill" ...

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding sentence is verbatim in the held Odden 1979 djvu (SLS 9(1):159-160, lines 9884-9888) and rule (6) is verbatim in the held Rosetta phonology excerpt of S&S 1960; the StressTyp2 entrycarries the same p.4 sentence independently, so the wording is doubly attested. (2) Deciding source: Sapir & Swadesh 1960:4, the grammatical introduction (by Swadesh from Sapir's notes) to the Yana Dictionary -- a grammar-sketch-grade primary and the only description of Yana stress that exists; every database and secondary source traces to it. Glottolog's 6 descriptive refs contain nothing better (Sapir 1922/1910/1923, held, give no placement rule; Hinton 1987/88 and Nevin 1976 are morphology). No instrumental or later phonological study is possible for new data (language extinct); the one later analytic work found is an unrecovered LSA 2002 abstract on Yahi stress exceptions.
